title: Genesis 6. The Cup Overflows.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 6. The Cup Overflows.
Man begins to multiply on the earth.
Daughters are born.
The sons of God see that the daughters of men are beautiful,
and they take wives for themselves, whoever they choose.
The grabbing that began in chapter three,
reaching for what was not given, has now multiplied into a pattern.
What was one hand reaching for one fruit is now an entire generation taking whatever it wants.
The Nephilim are on the earth in those days.
Mighty men.
Men of renown.
The Cup is not empty.
It is full,
but what it holds is no longer what was poured into it.
God says: My Spirit shall not strive with man forever.
He is flesh.
His days shall be a hundred and twenty years.
A clock begins.
Not because God is impatient, because the violence is becoming total.
The boundary God set at the door in chapter four,
the warning He gave Cain, sin crouching, you must rule over it,
has been ignored across generations.
Now the timer runs.
Grace has an edge.
The Cup that was filled with patience is reaching the lip.
The Lord sees that the wickedness of man is great on the earth.
Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart is only evil continually.
Not some evil.
Not occasional evil.
Every imagination.
Continually.
The vessel that was made for God's image is now filled with its own thoughts,
and they are all evil.
The Cup that received light and life and breath has been turned into something else entirely.
And the Lord was sorry that He had made man on the earth,
and it grieved Him at His heart.
This is not anger.
It is grief.
The word that describes God's response is the word for a wound,
a hurt that goes to the center.
The Cup that was filled at creation now overflows,
but what overflows is sorrow.
God is not detached from what He made.
He feels the weight of what it became.
The same God who spoke light into darkness and saw that it was good now looks at what He made and grieves.
He says:
I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the ground.
Man, animals, creeping things, birds of the sky.
For I am sorry that I have made them.
The judgment covers everything.
Not only man, all flesh.
The ground that was cursed, the animals that were given for food,
the birds that filled the sky on day five.
The Cup that was filled across six days will be emptied.
But Noah.
Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord.
The first time the word grace appears in Scripture,
it appears in the middle of total corruption.
Not in a garden.
Not at a mountain.
In a world where every imagination is only evil continually.
One man is seen.
Not because he earned it.
Because God looked, the same verb that was used in chapter one,
God saw the light, and saw that it was good,
is now used here: God looked at Noah.
Recognition is still something God gives by seeing.
Noah is a righteous man.
Blameless in his generation.
Noah walked with God.
The phrase that belonged to Enoch,
the man who was taken past death, now belongs to Noah.
The line that began calling on the name of the Lord in chapter four has produced a man who walks with God in a generation that does not.
The earth is corrupt before God.
The earth is filled with violence.
All flesh has corrupted its way on the earth.
God sees it.
He speaks to Noah:
The end of all flesh has come before Me.
The earth is filled with violence through them.
I will destroy them with the earth.
Then He gives instructions.
Make an ark of gopher wood.
Rooms in it.
Seal it inside and out with pitch.
Three hundred cubits long.
Fifty wide.
Thirty high.
A roof.
A door in the side.
Three decks.
The Cup that overflows with judgment also holds the survival of everything that will come after.
A vessel is designed, not to prevent the flood,
but to carry life through it.
God does not save Noah from the water.
He saves him in the water.
The ark is a cup inside the Cup,
a smaller vessel held inside the larger judgment,
designed to preserve what the larger one destroys.
I will bring the flood of waters on this earth,
to destroy all flesh having the breath of life.
Everything that is in the earth will die.
But I will establish My covenant with you.
The first time the word covenant appears in Scripture.
It appears inside judgment.
Not after it.
Before it.
Before the rain falls, before the ark is finished,
before the animals come,
God speaks a word that binds Him to a man.
The covenant is not the ark.
The covenant is the promise that the man and his family will survive what is coming.
The ark is the vessel.
The covenant is the word.
You shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife,
your sons' wives.
Of every living thing, two of every sort, male and female.
They shall come to you.
Birds, livestock, creeping things, two of every kind.
Take food.
Gather it.
The creatures will come.
Noah will receive them.
The man who walked with God will now hold the survival of every living thing inside a wooden vessel sealed with pitch.
Thus Noah did.
He did all that God commanded him.
The sentence is brief.
The work it describes is enormous,
but the text does not give the ark's construction duration here.
The Cup overflows.
But inside the overflow, one man builds a vessel.
What will happen when the door closes has not yet happened.
The rain has not yet begun.
